slides: Let's continue with plugging in numbers, and how to choose the number.

slides.say: The number must obey every condition in the question. If it says x is at least four, x can't be two.
at: If it says x is at least four

slides.say: If a is a positive whole number, it can't be zero, and it can't be a half. And if a letter is in the bottom of a fraction, it can't be zero, because we can't divide by zero.
at: If a is a positive whole number
in the bottom of a fraction

slides.say: In a figure, choose a value that looks right in the drawing. If an angle looks like about fifty degrees, don't plug in a hundred twenty.
And a good first try is often the edge of what's allowed. If x is at least four, try four itself.
Second, check that the choices come out different. Here's an example. x squared times x cubed, over x. The choices are x to the fourth, x to the fifth, x to the sixth, and x cubed.
Say I plug in x equals one. One to any power is one. So the question gives one, and all four choices give one too. Nothing is ruled out.
Zero does the same. Zero to any power is zero, so all four choices give zero. So zero and one often make the choices come out the same, and then they can't tell them apart.

Now x equals two. Two squared is four, and two cubed is eight. Four times eight is thirty-two, and thirty-two over two is sixteen. The choices give sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four and eight. They're all different, and only x to the fourth gives sixteen.

So before you calculate, look at the choices. If they have powers, products or fractions, skip zero and one, and start with two or three. When the choices are numbers, zero and one are fine, because there's nothing to tie.
Third, give different letters different numbers. Look at two choices, a squared b, and a b squared.
If a and b are both two, both choices give eight. Two squared times two is eight, and two times two squared is eight. They tie.
With a equals two and b equals three, a squared b is four times three, twelve. And a b squared is two times nine, eighteen. Now they're different.
Different letters may be equal, unless the question says they're not. But equal numbers often hide the difference, so we choose different ones.
Fourth, rule out three choices. Sometimes even a good number leaves two. For example, x times the bracket x plus one. The choices are x squared plus x, three x, x squared plus one, and four x.
Let's take x equals two. Two times three is six. x squared plus x is four plus two, six. Three x is six too. x squared plus one is five, out. And four x is eight, out.
at: x squared plus x is four plus two

slides: Two choices give six, so we can't decide yet. This is why we don't stop at the first choice that fits. We take a tie-breaker number, and we check only the two choices that are left. The ones that are out stay out.

slides.say: x equals three. Three times four is twelve. x squared plus x is nine plus three, twelve. Three x is nine, so it's out. The answer is x squared plus x. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
at: x squared plus x is nine plus three
